attribution.note: Zitron's own sentence in his own post. The Paris Marx citation comes after it and is not part of this claim.

semantics.note: The proposition faithfully covers all three parts: high cost, no profit yet, and investor indifference. It is a present-tense observation with no hedge.

contract.note: Limiting the claim to generative AI and reading indifference as general tolerance are both fair, ordinary readings. Because no profit basis is given and the financial and market parts need different windows, the verdict depends on interpretation.

evidence.note: Reuters (Jan 31, 2024): Nasdaq futures and megacap stocks fell on rising AI cost projections. This weighs against indifference, but it is one trading episode in parent-company shares, not broad evidence across the period.

reviews.rationale: There is no disaggregated evidence on generative AI profitability, so the financial part is unsettled. The single Reuters episode cuts against investor indifference. But the contract says individual price moves cannot show market-wide attitudes, so it does not meet the contradiction condition. The available evidence settles neither part.

semantics.note: The wording is verbatim and keeps the 'many problems' scope and 'can't even begin to fix'. It is an observation, but its concluding part is rhetorical and undefined.

contract.note: The contract rightly finds no stable whole-claim test. The set of promoted problems and the standard for 'beginning to fix' are unspecified, and choosing them would decide the verdict.

Measurements show generative tasks use more inference energy. This bears on 'costly', with no monetary comparator.
Copilot experiment (completed 2022) found faster coding on one bounded task. This does not refute failure on other unspecified problems.

reviews.rationale: The core assertion, that it is promoted for many problems it can't even begin to fix, names no set of problems and no standard of progress. The evidence touches only the narrow 'imperfect' and 'costly' parts. The claim as a whole is too vague to score.

attribution.note: Zitron's own sentence. The surrounding text identifies the advertiser as Microsoft (the Copilot ad).

semantics.note: The proposition keeps 'difficult to find' and 'couldn't seem to'. Naming Microsoft is supported by the context. It is an observation about a past ad.

contract.note: Focusing on whether the ad materially misrepresented results is a fair, ordinary reading. Requiring proof of knowing deception for 'outright lying' is strict but fits the word. Interpretation decides the verdict.

evidence.note: Tech Brew (Feb 22, 2024) reproduced the chemistry quiz, a tangible use case that worked. The logo and code tasks needed extra prompting and gave garbled text. Microsoft said the visible prompts were shortened. This is one uncontrolled test with no production records.

reviews.rationale: One journalistic test found one task worked as shown and others reachable only with more effort. That suggests the ad overstated ease, not that it was fabricated. With no production records, no controlled reproduction and no evidence of knowing deception, neither the support nor the contradiction condition is met.
